analysis.one_liner: Raises the salary cap under which salaried workers lose overtime pay, indexed to rise automatically.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote; it sat in the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current rules, most salaried workers who earn above $35,568 can be labeled 'executive, administrative, or professional' and lose their legal right to overtime pay. This bill would raise that salary cutoff to $45,000 on enactment, then step it up to $55,000, $65,000, and $75,000, and after 2027 tie it automatically to the 55th percentile of what full-time salaried workers earn nationally. It would also tighten the duties test so that an employee who spends 20% or more of their time on non-exempt work cannot be denied overtime. The bill was referred to the Senate labor committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Salaried workers earning between roughly $35,568 and the rising threshold — including many retail, office, health care, restaurant, and first-line supervisors — would regain the right to overtime pay for hours worked beyond 40 a week. The bill's findings note that in 1975 about 63 percent of full-time salaried workers were guaranteed overtime, versus under 15 percent under the 2019 rule; restoring the 55th-percentile threshold would push coverage back toward historic levels. All workers benefit indirectly if employers spread hours instead of overworking a salaried few.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the overtime-eligibility salary threshold in phases: $45,000 on enactment, $55,000 in 2024, $65,000 in 2025, $75,000 in 2026, and from 2027 tied to the 55th percentile of national weekly earnings for full-time salaried workers, updated automatically each year without new rulemaking.

Tightens the white-collar exemption so it no longer applies if at least 20 percent of an employee's duties are not directly or closely related to executive or administrative work, restoring coverage for working supervisors whose jobs are mostly hands-on.
Requires the Bureau of Labor Statistics to publish quarterly, by census region, data on weekly earnings of full-time salaried workers, making future threshold updates transparent.

analysis.who_pays: Employers — particularly retail, restaurant, health care, logistics, and other labor-intensive industries that rely on salaried managers working long hours without overtime — would face higher payroll costs, either by paying overtime or by raising salaries above the threshold to keep the exemption. Some workers could see hours capped or schedules shifted as employers adjust; small businesses with thin margins would bear disproportionate adjustment costs.

drawbacks.text: The phase-up to a $75,000 threshold and then an automatic index to the 55th percentile is a large, fast payroll increase for employers, especially small businesses and operators in lower-wage regions, who would need to either pay overtime, raise salaries, or restrict hours — with possible reductions in hours or staffing flexibility as a result.

The tighter 20 percent duties test would narrow who can keep the salaried exemption, requiring many employers to reclassify workers and add recordkeeping for hours worked, a real compliance burden the bill does not offset.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is substantial and targeted: millions of lower- and middle-income salaried workers would regain overtime rights that eroded because the threshold was not updated for decades. The costs are real but conventional — higher payroll for long-hours employers and reclassification work — and the multi-year phase-in gives employers time to adjust. The automatic indexation is the bill's strongest design feature, preventing the threshold from silently rotting again as it did between 1975 and 2019.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate HELP Committee on introduction day and stayed there; the committee never held a markup or sent it to the floor, and the two-year Congress ended with no vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on March 29, 2023, and it was read twice and referred the same day to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
That referral — read twice and referred to committee — is the entire recorded action history of the bill; no hearing, markup, committee report, or floor action appears in the record.
The bill never reached a floor vote in either chamber, so no roll-call was ever taken on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of long-hours salaried managers — in retail, restaurants, health care, and logistics — are better off, since they continue paying no overtime to exempt workers above the $35,568 threshold, while the workers who would have gained overtime rights are no better off than before.

for.name: Sen. Sherrod Brown
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Restoring Overtime Pay Act of 2023 in the Senate.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Schumer and 18 other Senate Democrats plus Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.role: Original cosponsors, including the Senate Majority Leader
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction, including the Majority Leader and Sen. Sanders (I-VT), who chaired the HELP Committee in the 118th Congress.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to committee on introduction day and never scheduled a hearing or markup, so it never left committee or reached the floor.

against.name: Senate leadership and the 118th Congress as a whole
against.what_they_did: No chamber of the 118th Congress took up the bill in the roughly 21 months remaining after introduction.

sides.party_line_note: All 20 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's Independent, with no Republican support recorded, and the bill's death in committee was a party-shaped outcome rather than a recorded partisan vote, since no vote was ever held.

industries.industry: Retail, restaurant, hospitality, and logistics employers
industries.note: These industries rely heavily on salaried managers and assistants who work long weeks without overtime pay once they earn above $35,568. The bill would force them to pay time-and-a-half beyond 40 hours or raise salaries to $75,000+, a direct payroll cost that instead stays with them as continued unpaid hours. As a result, the bill's death preserves their current cost structure at the expense of those workers' paychecks.

Large numbers of charge nurses, supervisors, and administrative staff earn salaries in the $36,000–$75,000 band and commonly work overtime; the bill would make those hours compensable, raising labor costs in a sector where residents' and patients' care depends on those hours. Keeping the bill bottled up leaves their workers' extra hours uncompensated.

The steepest threshold in decades would raise compliance and payroll costs most sharply for small firms with thin margins, a good-faith objection supporters would have to answer. The phase-in to 2026 and the exemption they currently enjoy mean the status quo the bill's death preserves favors them over their salaried employees.
